claims.text: Cooling history relative to intrinsic elemental interdiffusion kinetics primarily governs whether noble metal–based HEA nanoparticles form a single-phase solid solution or undergo phase separation.
A rapid quench locks in excessive thermal energy that induces local concentration fluctuations and elemental segregation.
An intermediate-temperature step-cooling stage permits partial atomic reordering and homogenization without causing full phase separation or uncontrolled particle growth.
Rapid heating and cooling often produce phase-separated, compositionally segregated, and morphologically uncontrolled noble metal–based HEA nanoparticles.
The proposed intervention replaces an immediate quench with a rapid drop to a moderate hold temperature followed by slower cooling to room temperature.
The intermediate hold should be placed just below the melting or critical homogenization temperature and selected according to constituent-element diffusion characteristics.
A hold temperature approximately 100–200 °C below the maximum processing temperature is an applicable example window.
A moderate hold during cooling permits controlled atomic interdiffusion and reduces local elemental concentration gradients.
Enhanced chemical homogenization creates more uniform nucleation sites that stabilize a single-phase solid solution.
The initial rapid cooling step suppresses high-temperature decomposition and morphological instabilities.
Limited atomic mobility during the subsequent cooling stage allows local compositions to readjust.
Local compositional readjustment minimizes kinetically trapped elemental clusters that would otherwise cause phase separation and uncontrolled morphology.
Step-cooled nanoparticles will have greater single-phase crystallinity and less elemental segregation than rapid-quenched nanoparticles.
Step-cooled nanoparticles will have more uniform particle morphology than rapid-quenched nanoparticles.
Step-cooled nanoparticles will have a lower apparent thermal decomposition temperature, which is asserted to indicate a thermodynamically stabilized solid solution.
The hypothesis applies when constituent elements have moderately similar diffusion kinetics and mixing enthalpies favor metastable solid-solution formation.
The hypothesis may not apply when constituent atomic mobilities differ extremely or compositions are far from the ideal configurational-entropy limit.
The optimal intermediate hold temperature and cooling rate depend on the noble-metal combination, synthesis scale, and reactor geometry.

Failure of step cooling to produce statistically significant improvements in phase purity and elemental uniformity together with a reduction in decomposition temperature relative to the rapid-quench control would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis treats a lower thermal decomposition temperature as evidence of greater thermodynamic stabilization, while assigning the less successful baseline a higher decomposition temperature. Ordinarily, easier decomposition is not itself evidence of greater thermal or thermodynamic stability, and no alternative definition of 'apparent decomposition temperature' is supplied.

The mediator invokes formation of uniform nucleation sites during a cooling hold described as occurring after a drop from a synthesis regime where melting or high diffusion has already been achieved. It is unclear whether nucleation has already occurred before the proposed hold, making the stated sequence internally ambiguous.
